question.problem: If ${f}^{′}(x)=|x+5|,$ which of the following could be the graph of a continuous function $y=f(x)?$
question.worked_solution:
The graph of $y={f}^{′}(x)$ is the following:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14200695/assets/ae96c488c78fb207567c6ae0ea7497782af1e840a7852bd79b57902d45972a01.png)

Recall that critical points of $y=f(x)$ occur when ${f}^{′}(x)=0$ or ${f}^{′}(x)$ does not exist. In our case, there is one critical point: 

$\,$ $x=-5$ 

Also, we have the following: 

- If ${f}^{′}(x)>0$ then $f(x)$ is increasing.

- If ${f}^{′}(x)<0$ then $f(x)$ is decreasing.

We can now summarize the information from the graph in the table below.

| $x$ | $(-\infty ,-5)$ | $-5$ | $(-5,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${f}^{′}$ | $+$ | $0$ | $+$ |
| $f$ | $↗$ | $\text{no extr.}$ | $↗$ |

Let's now sketch the graph of $y=f(x):$

- First, we draw the critical point. We choose an arbitrary point on the vertical line $x=-5,$ as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14200695/assets/2c67c136914eba7687d96a66e737e2f1f7d96144d4535b25f0ac48e16aed8396.png)

- Next, we consider the behavior of $y=f(x)$ in the neighborhood of the critical points:

- Since $f(x)$ is increasing $↗$ on $(-\infty ,-5)$ and on $(-5,\infty )$, the graph of $y=f(x)$ goes down to the left of $x=-5$ and goes up to the right of $x=-5.$

- Furthermore, since ${f}^{′}(x)$ is decreasing to the left of $x=-5$, we must have ${f}^{″}(x)<0$, and, since it is increasing to the right of $x=-5$, we must have ${f}^{″}(x)>0.$ So, $x=-5$ is an inflection point at which the curve $y=f(x)$ changes from concave down to concave up.

So, we can draw as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14200695/assets/971e495bbe1d7c502a1e65ec2b0764f0057158e3fe989261245382223020e872.png)

- Finally, since we are told that our graph must be continuous, by connecting and extending the existing parts with a smooth curve, we obtain a possible graph of $y=f(x):$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14200695/assets/00320e4c614d3ba3051ffca74a005113b057668488c12d50c5c497d613ce7492.png)

**Note:** The graph we obtained is not the only possible one. Any similar graph that's shifted vertically up or down could also be considered a possible $y=f(x).$
